name: mistletoe

attributes.attribute: an evergreen parasitic plant, the species Viscum album
the most sacred plant of the druids when grown on an oak
harvested with a golden sickle and called all-heal
kept out of churches for its pagan links

sources: Crow, W. B. “The Mistletoe Sacrament.” In Matthews, John. A Celtic Reader: Selections from Celtic Legend, Scholarship and Story. Wellingborough: Aquarian Press, 1991.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Mistletoe is an evergreen parasitic plant that grows on deciduous trees and shrubs. The European kind is the species Viscum album. The plant keeps ancient symbolic force even now. In Britain and America people still hang a sprig at the winter holidays and kiss beneath it. The link between mistletoe and pre-Christian religion is firm enough that the plant is not used in church decorations. People once held it sacrilegious to bring it into a church. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder said mistletoe was the most sacred plant of the druids, especially when it grew on an oak, a tree holy to the Celtic priesthood. Pliny said the plant was cut with a golden sickle on the sixth day after the new moon. After a ritual banquet, two white bulls with bound horns were led to the tree and slaughtered. A mistletoe so harvested, called all-heal, was used as a medicine against barrenness and impotence and as a remedy for poisons.

okr.objective: Document mistletoe and its sacred power among the Celts.
